title: nCr mod p
directAnswer: You can't compute n! / (r!·(n−r)!) then take mod p, because the division isn't valid in modular arithmetic and n! overflows. The fix when p is prime and p > n: precompute factorials fact[0..n] mod p and their modular inverses, then nCr mod p = fact[n] · invFact[r] · invFact[n−r] mod p. The inverse comes from Fermat's little theorem: a⁻¹ ≡ a^(p−2) (mod p). Precompute in O(n) (one pass for factorials, one inverse via Fermat, then a backward pass), and answer each query in O(1).

remember.pattern: Precomputed factorials + modular inverse via Fermat's little theorem
remember.formula:
fact[0]=1; fact[i]=fact[i-1]*i % p
invFact[n]=modpow(fact[n], p-2, p)        # Fermat
for i from n-1 down to 0: invFact[i]=invFact[i+1]*(i+1) % p
nCr = fact[n] * invFact[r] % p * invFact[n-r] % p
rules: **Never** compute n!/(r!(n−r)!) with integer division then mod — division isn't modular; multiply by the modular **inverse** instead.
Fermat's little theorem needs p **prime** and gcd(a, p) = 1: then a^(p−1) ≡ 1, so a⁻¹ ≡ a^(p−2) (mod p).
Compute all inverse-factorials with **one** modpow: invert fact[n] once, then walk backward `invFact[i] = invFact[i+1]·(i+1)`. Don't run modpow n times.
Return 0 immediately if `r < 0` or `r > n` — nCr is 0 there, and indexing invFact[n−r] with a negative index is a bug.
Take mod after **every** multiplication and use **long** in Java — `fact[i-1]*i` and the triple product exceed 32 bits well before n is large.
whenToUse: Many binomial-coefficient queries nCr mod p with a fixed prime modulus (often 1e9+7)
n is up to ~10⁶–10⁷ and p is prime with p > n
Counting problems (paths, sequences, distributions) reduced to binomials under a prime mod
You need O(1) per query after an O(n) precompute
antiSignals: n is larger than p (or p is small) → Fermat indexing breaks; use **Lucas' theorem** instead
The modulus is **not prime** → Fermat doesn't apply; use extended GCD inverses or CRT over prime-power factors
You need exact (non-modular) huge binomials → big integers, Pascal's triangle, no inverse trick
Only a single small nCr is needed → multiplicative formula with divide-as-you-go is enough
remember.takeaway: Binomials under a prime mod are a two-line idea once you accept that 'division' becomes 'multiply by the modular inverse'. Precompute factorials forward, invert the top factorial once with Fermat, then sweep inverses backward — O(n) setup, O(1) queries. The trap is reaching for integer division; the fix is Fermat's a^(p−2). When n exceeds p, this breaks and Lucas takes over.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know that modular division must go through a modular inverse, that Fermat's little theorem supplies that inverse when p is prime, and that all inverse-factorials can be derived from a single modpow in O(n).
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Computing n!/(r!(n−r)!) with integer division before taking mod (wrong and overflowing), or calling modpow once per query (turning O(1) answers into O(log p) each, and the precompute into O(n log p)).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the inverse from Fermat out loud (a^(p−1) ≡ 1 ⇒ a⁻¹ ≡ a^(p−2)), and show the backward sweep invFact[i] = invFact[i+1]·(i+1) that needs only one modpow for the whole table.

problemStatement:
Given integers `n`, `r`, and a **prime** modulus `p` with `p > n`, compute the binomial coefficient

`C(n, r) = n! / (r! · (n − r)!)`  taken modulo `p`.

You will answer **many** such queries against the same `p` (commonly `p = 1\,000\,000\,007`). Preprocess once so each query is `O(1)`. Define `C(n, r) = 0` when `r < 0` or `r > n`.
constraints: 0 ≤ r ≤ n ≤ 10⁶ (precompute factorial tables of this size)
p is prime and p > n (so Fermat's inverse applies and no factor of p appears in n!)
p ≤ 10⁹ + 7 (typical), products fit in 64-bit after each mod
Many queries → O(n) precompute, O(1) per query is required
Return 0 for r < 0 or r > n
understanding: C(n, r) counts subsets of size r from n items, but we want it modulo a prime p, not exactly. Two obstacles: n! is astronomically large (overflow), and the formula divides — and division is not a native modular operation. We fix both at once. Work in arithmetic mod p so numbers stay small, and replace each division by multiplication with a modular inverse. Because p is prime, Fermat's little theorem gives the inverse as a power, and one clever backward pass produces every inverse-factorial cheaply.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is p prime, and is p larger than n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes on both — that's the regime where Fermat's inverse works and no factor of p divides into n!. If n could exceed p, I'd switch to Lucas' theorem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many queries, and what's the max n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Many queries (that's why we precompute), with n up to ~10⁶. So O(n) setup and O(1) per query, not O(log p) per query.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should C(n, r) be when r is out of range?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 0 for r < 0 or r > n. I guard that first so I never index a factorial table with a negative or oversized index.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What modulus should I assume?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Usually 1e9+7, which is prime. The method works for any prime p > n; I'll keep p as a parameter.

examples.explanation: C(5,2) = 10, and 10 < p so the answer is just 10. fact[5]=120, invFact[2]·invFact[3] reconstruct 120/(2·6)=10.
C(10,3) = 120, and 120 mod 13 = 3. Note p = 13 > n = 10, so Fermat applies.
r > n, so C(4,5) = 0 by definition — guarded before any table lookup.

approaches.name: Direct Factorial Division (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention first to expose the two traps — overflow and invalid modular division — that the optimal method removes.
hints: The textbook formula is n! / (r! (n−r)!). The most direct code multiplies out the factorials and divides. What two things go wrong when we add 'mod p'?
n! overflows fast — 21! already exceeds a 64-bit integer. And taking mod of a quotient is not the quotient of the mods: (a / b) mod p ≠ (a mod p) / (b mod p).

Even computing the factorials mod p doesn't save you, because once you've reduced numerator and denominator mod p you can no longer divide them — division isn't defined in modular arithmetic without an inverse.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Multiplying n factors for the factorials is O(n) per query, with O(1) extra space. But the real problem is correctness: without modular inverses you either overflow (no mod) or compute a meaningless quotient (mod then divide).
approaches.explanation:
The literal translation of the formula multiplies the numerator `n!`, multiplies the denominator `r!·(n−r)!`, and divides. Adding 'mod p' to this breaks in two distinct ways.

**Trap 1 — overflow without mod.** `n!` grows faster than any fixed-width integer. `21!` already overflows 64 bits, so for any interesting `n` the numerator is garbage long before you divide. Big integers avoid the overflow but make every query slow and miss the point of working mod p.

**Trap 2 — division is not modular.** Suppose you reduce numerator and denominator mod p to keep them small. Now you're stuck: `(a / b) mod p` is **not** `(a mod p) / (b mod p)`. Concretely, `(10 / 2) mod 7 = 5`, but `(10 mod 7) / (2 mod 7) = 3 / 2`, which isn't even an integer. Modular arithmetic has no native division; you can only multiply. So a mod-as-you-go factorial leaves you unable to perform the final divide.

**The fix the optimal uses.** Division by `b` modulo `p` must become multiplication by `b⁻¹`, the modular inverse of `b`. Since `p` is prime, that inverse exists for every `b` not divisible by `p` and is given by Fermat's little theorem. That single substitution — divide becomes multiply-by-inverse — is what makes the whole computation valid mod p.
approaches.insight: The baseline fails not because it's slow but because it's wrong under a modulus: you cannot divide in modular arithmetic. The entire optimal method is one idea — replace ÷b with ×b⁻¹ — plus precomputation so each inverse is cheap.

approaches.name: Precomputed Factorials + Fermat Inverse (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with 'division becomes multiply-by-inverse, and Fermat gives the inverse since p is prime'.

complexity.time: O(n + log p) precompute, O(1) per query

hints: C(n, r) = fact[n] · (fact[r])⁻¹ · (fact[n−r])⁻¹ mod p. The only hard part is the inverse — what does Fermat's little theorem say about a⁻¹ when p is prime?
Fermat: a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p) for a not divisible by p, so a⁻¹ ≡ a^(p−2) (mod p) via fast modular exponentiation.
You don't need n separate modpow calls. Invert fact[n] once, then invFact[i] = invFact[i+1]·(i+1) mod p going backward — because (i!)⁻¹ = ((i+1)!)⁻¹ · (i+1).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building fact[0..n] is O(n) multiplications. One Fermat inverse via fast exponentiation is O(log p). The backward sweep for invFact is another O(n). So precompute is O(n + log p); every query is three O(1) array lookups and two multiplications.
approaches.explanation:
Work entirely in arithmetic modulo `p` and replace the single division in the binomial formula with multiplication by modular inverses.

**The formula in modular form.** `C(n, r) = fact[n] · invFact[r] · invFact[n−r] (mod p)`, where `fact[i] = i! mod p` and `invFact[i] = (i!)⁻¹ mod p`. Every value stays in `[0, p)`, so nothing overflows once we reduce after each multiply.

**Why Fermat gives the inverse.** `p` is prime, and any `a` with `1 ≤ a < p` satisfies `gcd(a, p) = 1`. Fermat's little theorem then says `a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p)`. Multiply both sides by `a⁻¹`: `a^(p−2) ≡ a⁻¹ (mod p)`. So the inverse of any factorial is just that factorial raised to the `p−2` power, computed with fast modular exponentiation in `O(log p)`. (This needs `p > n` so that no `i ≤ n` is a multiple of `p` — otherwise `fact[i]` would be `0 mod p` and have no inverse.)

**Why one modpow is enough for all inverses.** Calling `a^(p−2)` for every factorial would be `O(n log p)` — wasteful. Instead invert only the top: `invFact[n] = fact[n]^(p−2) mod p`. Then use the relation `(i!)⁻¹ = ((i+1)!)⁻¹ · (i+1)` (since `(i+1)! = (i+1)·i!`, inverting both sides gives this). Sweeping `i` from `n−1` down to `0` fills the whole `invFact` table with one multiplication each — a single modpow for the entire array.

**Why each query is O(1).** After the tables exist, a query is `fact[n] · invFact[r] mod p · invFact[n−r] mod p` — two multiplications and a couple of mods. Guard `r < 0 || r > n` first and return `0`, both because the coefficient is genuinely `0` there and because `invFact[n−r]` with a negative index would crash.

**Why overflow-safe.** Each product of two values `< p` (with `p ≈ 10⁹`) is up to `~10¹⁸`, which fits in a signed 64-bit `long` — but only if you take `mod p` after **every** multiplication so it never compounds. Python integers are unbounded, so the mod is for speed and to match the math, not to prevent overflow.
approaches.insight: The whole method is the substitution 'divide by b' → 'multiply by b^(p−2)', made cheap by precomputation. The elegant trick is deriving the entire inverse-factorial table from a single modpow via the backward recurrence — turning what looks like n exponentiations into n multiplications. Remember the precondition p > n and prime; the moment n can exceed p, Fermat's indexing breaks and Lucas' theorem takes over.

The single Fermat inverse: (n!)⁻¹ ≡ (n!)^(p−2). One modpow for the whole table.
Backward sweep using (i!)⁻¹ = ((i+1)!)⁻¹·(i+1); turns n exponentiations into n multiplications.

java.line: return fact[n] * invFact[r] % p * invFact[n - r] % p;
java.explanation: The modular binomial: divide became multiply-by-inverse. Mod between the two products keeps everything < p².

python.explanation: Built-in pow(base, p−2, p) is Fermat's inverse in O(log p).
Backward recurrence fills every inverse-factorial from the one above it.

python.line: if r < 0 or r > n: return 0
python.explanation: Out-of-range guard before any table access.

pitfalls: Calling modpow once per factorial inverse — O(n log p); the backward sweep needs only one modpow.
Forgetting mod after a multiply — the long overflows or Python slows on huge ints.
Skipping the r < 0 / r > n guard — wrong value and a negative index into invFact.
Using Fermat when p is not prime, or when n ≥ p — both break; use Lucas or extended-GCD inverses.
Using int in Java for fact/invFact products — overflow; everything must be long.

edgeCases.behavior: invFact[0] = 1, so both equal fact[n]·1·invFact[n] = 1, the correct value.
Fine as long as n < p; if n ≥ p, fact has a 0 factor and the method is invalid — use Lucas.

commonMistakes: Computing n!/(r!(n−r)!) with integer division then taking mod — division isn't modular.
Running a modpow for every inverse-factorial instead of one modpow + backward sweep.
Forgetting to reduce mod p after each multiplication, causing overflow in Java.
Using Fermat's inverse when p is not prime or when n ≥ p.
Not guarding r < 0 / r > n, producing wrong answers and negative indices.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Dividing instead of multiplying by the inverse
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Modular arithmetic has no division. (a / b) mod p is not (a mod p) / (b mod p); the correct operation is a · b⁻¹ mod p, where b⁻¹ comes from Fermat.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return fact[n] * invFact[r] % p * invFact[n - r] % p; // multiply by inverses

commonMistakesDetailed.title: One modpow per factorial inverse
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Inverting every factorial separately is O(n log p). Inverting only fact[n] and sweeping backward with (i!)⁻¹ = ((i+1)!)⁻¹·(i+1) costs one modpow plus O(n) multiplies.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: inv_fact = [pow(self.fact[i], p - 2, p) for i in range(max_n + 1)]  # O(n log p)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
inv_fact = [1] * (max_n + 1)
inv_fact[max_n] = pow(self.fact[max_n], p - 2, p)
for i in range(max_n - 1, -1, -1):
    inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i + 1] * (i + 1) % p

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing mod after a multiply (overflow)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: fact[i-1] * i without an immediate % p compounds across iterations and overflows a 64-bit long quickly; the table fills with garbage.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i;        // no mod — overflows long
commonMistakesDetailed.good: fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % p;    // reduce after every multiply

followupVariations.title: Lucas' Theorem
followupVariations.hint: When n ≥ p (or p is small), split n and r into base-p digits and multiply digit-wise nCr mod p.

followupVariations.title: Modular Exponentiation
followupVariations.hint: The a^(p−2) Fermat inverse is one modpow call — the engine behind invFact[n].

followupVariations.title: Extended Euclidean Algorithm
followupVariations.hint: If the modulus isn't prime, get inverses from extended GCD instead of Fermat.

followupVariations.title: Catalan Numbers
followupVariations.hint: Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n+1) mod p uses exactly this factorial-inverse machinery.

patternNote: Precomputed factorials with modular inverse. The default for many binomial queries under a fixed prime mod. Recognise it whenever a counting answer reduces to nCr mod p with p prime and p > n; the same fact/invFact tables power Catalan numbers, stars-and-bars counts, and inclusion–exclusion sums mod p.
